# **Mnookin Two-Pager Template and Examples**

Supplement to the book *[Never Search Alone](https://www.amazon.com/Never-Search-Alone-Seekers-Playbook/dp/B0B9Q9YDQ5)*  
By Phyl Terry  
All Rights Reserved

Creating a *draft* of what you want, what you don’t want, and what you love is an important first step before beginning your listening tour, or your “market research” on the intersection between what you want and what the market wants.

Remember, though, this is a draft. 

You do not have to get this right *before* beginning the listening tour.

In fact, the tour is meant to help you not only understand the market but get clarity on what *you* want and how the market sees you. 

This is the iterative (not waterfall) process I advocate for job seekers.

Read through and get inspired by what others have done.

Good luck\!

- Phyl

# Suggestions for use {#suggestions-for-use}

(With gratitude to Justin Meats for sharing his experience)

* Don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good. JUST START\!  
* Spend 15-30 minutes getting as many ideas of loves & hates as you can \- Call it a “draft.”  
* Share your “draft” with your JSC and get feedback \- Calling it a first draft takes the pressure off and helps you be vulnerable with a new group of People.  It’s not complete, but your JSC will help bring clarity, especially in how you describe it to others.  
* Spend 15-30 minutes updating and then transforming the love & hates into a “draft” of must-haves and must-nots  
* Share your “draft” of must-haves and must-nots with your JSC and get feedback  
* Update based on the feedback  
* Share your two-pager, “draft V2”  with your JSC and get feedback  
* Start your listening tour and share your “draft” on the tour \- do not send it out for email feedback.  
* Depending on the relationship and how well you know the person, you might choose to share the two-pager. Other times you might just hit the highlights verbally.  
* Remember to stay quiet, listen and follow up with probing questions, not statements like you know it all.  
* Update the two-pager after each meeting and share the changes with your JSC  
* Once you notice you’re not making many changes to the two-pager, you know you are close while you finalize your candidate market fit.   
* Don’t let the perfect be the enemy of the good before you start to share with recruiters either \- keep your momentum  
* Lean on your JSC the whole way through\!


## Your Mnookin Two-Pager has four sections {#your-mnookin-two-pager-has-four-sections}

1. What you love and hate doing   
2. Your “must-haves”  
3. Your “must-nots”  
4. Your strengths and weaknesses  
5. Your career goals (short-term and long-term)

## 1\. What you love and hate doing {#1.-what-you-love-and-hate-doing}

Here again is the exercise in the book to help you determine what you love and hate doing.

1. **Pair up with a member of your JSC.**

2. **Interview each other about what you hate doing.**   
   When you are paired up, interview each other about all the kinds of jobs, industries, functions, etc. that you hate and things you do not love doing. What about past jobs did you dislike? Why? Your partner should take notes on what you don’t like doing. Then, in the next steps, you will get the copy of their notes to review it.

3. **Review your list separately.**  
   Get your list of what you hate doing from your partner in this exercise. Each of you spend 15 minutes reviewing your own lists and adding anything.

4. **Invert focus to what you love doing.**  
   Now each of you invert your own lists. If you put down that you hate business travel, then invert that to you love jobs with little travel (and try to get more specific — maybe, you love running teams in one location, rather than national or global teams). Keep in mind that if you hate doing something, you will not always necessarily like or love doing the inverse. You may just be satisfied with the absence of the thing. 

In this exercise, be as open and honest as you can. Keep in mind that you can be good at something but not love it. For example, I’m quite good at finance, but coming out of Harvard Business School, I made a very clear choice not to go to Wall Street. I did not like the typical 1990s macho culture of those firms.

Also, look for opportunities to be creative. 

Let’s say you love to travel but do not like business travel. Could you find a way to combine those two things and improve your work/life balance in a way that you love your job more?

Once you have done this exercise, now move to the “Must-Nots.” This is a related but different exercise. There is some overlap, but here, you are going the next level down. Maybe you know that you love media and would love to work for a streaming company in a marketing role that requires little travel. 

## 2: The Must-Nots Exercise {#2:-the-must-nots-exercise}

 

1. **Pair up with a different member of your JSC.**

2. **Interview each other about what you do not want.**  
   When you are paired up, interview each other about all the things you do not want in your next job. For example, you might say that you don’t want to manage more than 10 people, you don’t want a boss who micromanages, etc.

3. **Use what I call the “bad bosses” prompt.**  
   If you are having any trouble getting your partner to articulate “must-nots,” then ask them again about past roles — “Have you ever had a bad job or a bad boss? If yes, what did that teach you about what you do not want in a boss, culture, etc.?”  
     
4. **Review your lists with each other.**

   
The irony of inverting and looking at the negative is that it’s a positive and fun experience.

## 

## 3: Your Must-Haves {#3:-your-must-haves}

   
Most job seekers tend *not* to think about their Must-Haves, especially if they are out of work.  
   
That’s a mistake. You’ll want to go through the process of determining your must-haves.  
   
So, with the same partner from the second exercise, run through these steps.  
 

1. **Review your Must-Nots.**  
   Begin this exercise by reviewing your partner’s Must-Nots from the last exercise. Again, these can be a road map to your must-haves.  
      
2. **Reverse the Must-Nots into Must-Haves.**  
   Then help your partner invert their Must-Nots into potential Must-Haves. For example, if a Must-Not is “frequent travel,” then a Must-Have would be something like “travel no more than once a month.”  
      
3. **Each separately refine your Must-Haves.**  
   Then you should each review the first pass on your Must-Haves that your partner created for you, and make any edits or changes.  
      
4. **Present your Must-Haves for Discussion.**  
   Then return to your partner and present your Must-Haves for discussion and feedback. Discuss each item. Ask what might be missing or should be edited.

## 4: Your Strengths and Weakness {#4:-your-strengths-and-weakness}

Think about your strengths and weaknesses. What do you think you are particularly good at doing? List that as a strength. Note: You may not like doing that thing but list it anyway. 

Where are you weak (and these may be things you’ve already identified you don’t like or are must-nots but put them down or may be things you want to improve upon)?

## 

## 5: Your Career Goals {#5:-your-career-goals}

Look over the results of the three exercises above, and then sit down and ask yourself, “What kind of job do I want now and in the long run?”  
   
Do you want to get promoted from Director of Product to VP of Product?  
   
Do you want to become a Chief Operating Officer or a CEO?  
   
Whatever the answers are, write down both your short-term career goal (i.e., what kind of job do you want next) and your long-term career goal (i.e., what you want eventually).  
   
Don’t worry if you are not sure what your short- or long-term goals are.  
   
Remember, this is a *draft*. 

Your Listening Tour will help you not only understand the market, but also understand *yourself* and what you want. 

Now let’s look at some examples of Two-Pagers from other job seekers.

# Templates {#templates}

There are two basic templates which you can consider using:

1. The unstructured one used for most of the examples in this document, or  
2. This structure table below or [spreadsheet-based version](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1R7gaVhsY3Ysv4i2--KDHPU4bzQ4JEnbRdYDn_oXi0Io/edit?usp=sharing) created by Maris Garcia (thanks Maris), which also comes with a bonus tool for managing your gratitude house and listening tour.

| What I hate doing |   |
| :---- | :---- |
| **What I love doing (and which of those are my strengths)** |   |
| **My must-nots** |   |
| **My must-haves**  |   |
| **Career goals: Short term** |   |
| **Career goals: Long term** |   |

# Examples of *Drafts* (not to be shared publicly necessarily) {#examples-of-drafts-(not-to-be-shared-publicly-necessarily)}

## Individual Contributor {#individual-contributor}

### Product Manager {#product-manager}

| *The below two-pager is longer than two pages. This product manager used her two-pager as an opportunity to think about what she wants and also how she has struggled in her career.  Then she went out and did a great listening tour and filled in quotes and key insights from her market research, which eventually led to the finished document you see below. This is a great approach and one you might consider duplicating. Note that her listening tour gave her great clarity on her candidate-market fit, and she subsequently turned down 4 offers she would have previously accepted (which was a big win for her – ability to avoid past mistakes), and eventually landed a great job at a well-funded, well-run startup that met all of the must-haves that she outlined below (including a company well-funded enough that she doesn’t have to worry about fundraising in the short-run and has room to experiment and fail). One recent job seeker said he found the Mnookin Two-Pager exercise to be too generic, akin to corporate mission/vision statements. I shared this example with him to show how to do it in a very clear and specific way that can guide your listening tour (and reflect what you learn), and eventually guide the roles you turn down on the way to finding a great job.* |
| :---- |

**Strengths** 

* **Vision Setting:**   
  * Quotes from managers:  
    * When I hear \[Name\] talk about the future of our product, I'm always excited. \[Name\]'s ability to create and share an inspiring vision makes me really proud to work for \[Company\], and more importantly, to work on the iPad team. I also appreciate how \[Name\] provides a rationale for her vision: if we're not pursuing a certain product feature, \[Name\] always has a logical reason why.  
    * I was constantly inspired and impressed by her ability to innovate, think outside the box, and bring big ideas to life through our product teams. \[Name\] has an infectious energy that attracts top talent to join her team. I learned so much by collaborating with \[Name\] — she approaches everything she does by taking a data-driven, research-based, strategic approach…”  
* **Discovery:**   
  * I love doing product discovery, validating ideas through and through.   
    * I think it's awesome that \[Name\] is a huge advocate for user centered product development. I really appreciate how much time she's spent talking with, observing, and trying to understand the needs of teachers/administrators/students over the past few months. I have not had this experience at other jobs. Her commitment to this cause has permeated throughout our team. I also appreciate that we're working with a discovery coach to figure out how to do better user centered product development”  
    * Seriously, you have an amazing ability to frame problems, and all the research you did really shone through.  
* **Continuous Learning Self / Others:**   
  * “\[Name\] constantly brings in new processes, ideas, articles that directly relate to our design work. Whether it’s hugely impactful changes to our design and dev processes, or a relevant article she finds and passes on.”  
    * Provided the team with a framework. Did a lot of the heavy lifting on the strategy work via guiding policies, pushing for external voices, rallying the team around a direction I wasn’t initially in favor of, outlining product teams, developing and rallying a team around Objectives.  
* **Organization Builder:**   
  * \[Name\] cares deeply about the culture of an organization, which led her to excel as an organizational leader.  
    * Impact on the organization (e.g. OKRs, goal setting, process, forcing tough convos etc.)   
* **Who I’ve worked well with:**   
  * Engineers (e.g….)  
  * Designers (e.g….)   
  * Sales leaders (e.g…)  
* **Times I most enjoyed/proud of:**   
* Creating / building towards the social growth strategy for \[Company\] and seeing the kids/kidfluencers and company/board get excited and gain traction  
* Shepherding \[Company\] through pivot from in-person to virtual and launching tons of stuff that supported that \- e.g. digital missions, badges, guide video etc.   
* Launching \[Company\] Assignments and seeing results / teacher enthusiasm for it  
* Working on \[Product Name\] with \[Person) and the narrow focused vision around it   
* Working on \[Product Name\] when we had the team staffed and were churning and building and the excitement of launching it and getting and iterating on the feedback

I think I’ve done my best work when:

* I have been able to focus and devote my time and energy to a problem space  
* Company (marketing, sales, eng etc.)  is aligned on single strategy / direction so there’s less competition / competing for resources and more figuring how to do it

**Areas I’ve Struggled with:** 

**Finding Product-Market Fit**

* At \[Company\] \- (from CEO) “We have early promising signs, but the company bookings and position in the market aren't reflecting a product with clear product market fit or "must have."  
* At \[Company\] \- my assessment \- We survived \[Company\] but the product-market fit isn’t there for a high-growth business in the potential in the coding classes. We are building towards the social vision but it’s slow and fundraising / leadership may not be there to get there in next 1-2 years.   
* My role in falling short here   
  * Focused too much on “new” only vs. “core”/”existing” users.   
    * E.g. \[New Product\] vs. the retention / engagement / improve the core work (eg ongoing products)  
  * Fell to escalation of commitment  
    * While initially had the right skepticism around \[Product\], felt the escalation of commitment once I was in and wanted to keep iterating when it was clear it wasn’t working  
  * Underestimated ability to pivot   
    * Believed in product led growth \[i.e., Products\], but didn’t believe we could fully transition and commit to it at \[Company\] within a b2b org or how quickly it would grow. 


**Delivery**

* I'd encourage her to balance that out more with product delivery   
* Ultimately, I think \[Name\]'s strengths lie in the bigger picture, visionary things and less in project management.

**Process/People** 

* Good at rallying team around strategy/vision/why, but struggled sometimes to turn up team morale if there were a couple naysayers (e.g. \[Names\] at \[Company\])  
* Sometimes loose with process doesn’t work well with people who like a more rigidly defined and followed process e.g. sprint planning / retro / 1:1s 

**Must have in a future role**

1. **Resources**   
   - Enough ppl/resources to bet BIG and still be ok if it fails.   
   - Not worried about layoffs or lots more fundraising to stay afloat.   
2. **Scale**   
   - Big enough product user base to learn from in a data driven, experimental way.  
3. **Focus & Growth**   
   - Inspiring product leader I can learn and grow from   
   - Wear “less hats” / own big, exciting scope but smaller than entire product / company survival  
   - Ideally work with small team of PMs (2-6 person) and don’t own as much of QA/delivery process   
   - Strong cross-functional counterparts that own w/ hiring, career paths, eng/design management etc. so I can focus on building/growing an awesome product or product area.   
4. **Mission \-** Company is working on a problem I care about solving and doing so in a hard-to-copy, technologically interesting way.   
5. **Work Culture \-** Remote first, humble but willing to engage in healthy conflict, written / async is a big part of communication style.  
6. **Product culture:** Dedicated product team org structure, launch and iterate, data & user insight driven.  
7. **Industry \-** Ideally not in a highly regulated environment so big results could happen in months vs. years. I like productivity / remote tools / creator economy / creator platforms / media, Bottoms up B2B or B2C, ideally SAAS or marketplace

### Product Manager {#product-manager-1}

**Love Doing**

* Creating tools or services improving people’s jobs/lifes  
* Working in quick iterations, incl. tests, prototypes, etc.  
* Mapping journeys, value chains, flows, etc.  
* Discovering user-centric & unusual solutions (in complex fields) (Methods)  
* Talking to / understanding users  
* Working with a diverse and cross-functional team  
* Working on a complex product  
* Discovering & delivering small things and understanding if they work  
* Utilizing my background in UX Design to guide a team on customer-focus  
* Diving deep to get a full picture  
* Deep work (Time and space to think deeply about problems)  
* Workshops  
* Discussing strategy  
* Looking also at how to work  
* Reflection & Learning (Methods, Tools, Mindset, etc.)  
* Teaching / Sharing / Discussing methods, approaches, and ways of working  
  **Hate Doing**  
* An Organization not focused on Outcomes, just being driven by feature delivery.  
* Being in a (product-cultural) immature environment  
* Disconnected from Team by managing 3rd party teams, off-/nearshore teams, managing contracts, etc.  
* Writing PRDs to hand them over to a 'team' (handover culture in general / waterfall approach)  
* Sitting around with 'meeting people' (middle-management driven culture)  
* Playing political theatre (internal politics driven by egos instead of balancing different interests for a common goal)  
* Executing on things I don't understand why  
* Being told to 'just do X' without any reasoning  
* Just managing technical debt and maintenance  
* Wasteful working with too big bets on unclear problems  
  **Must-Haves**  
* Strong product culture (Vision, Strategy & Execution)  
* Great direct Manager, from whom I can learn  
* Digital-First / Product Led  
* Learning environment  
* Space & trust for real product discovery  
* Motivated Team  
* Positive organization, people like being there  
* Social aspect (Office, Co-Working, similar)  
* Flexible working environment (hours, collaboration type)  
* Good pay  
* Interesting body of work  
* The product is still in the innovation stage, not already in maintenance  
  **Must-Nots**  
* Command & Control culture  
* An environment of inner politics, personal agendas, toxic egos  
* An organization without aptitude for working strategically  
* Prescribed crazy working hours (just to show attendance)  
* A company that is mainly sales or marketing driven  
* Too extensive traveling  
* Company in early stages of culture/digital transformation  
* Company in optimization game

  #### 

  #### 

  **Career Goals**  
  **Short term**  
* (Senior) Product Management Job in a successful tech company with strong product culture. The product should be in the productivity space. I want to see one of these from the inside to learn from great people to and check my own maturity. As a side effect I want to earn credibility in my craft.  
  **Long term**  
* Go into consulting/coaching/teaching for product people with a focus on visual thinking.  
* Go into general consulting/teaching for complex topics with visual thinking.  
* Teaching mapping / visual thinking methods and approaches. With some product approach (courses, material, software)  
* Alternative: Continue career in product management in the direction of people management.

### Product Manager {#product-manager-2}

| *This candidate (Claudia is not her real name) is seeking to pivot from general B2C product management to health tech/mental health tech. As she went through her Listening tour, she included comments from her interviewees that supported her strengths.* |
| :---- |

**Candidate Market Fit Statement**  
I’m looking for a Sr/Principal/Dir PM role in the mental health tech space where the focus is on the patient- or provider-facing experience and the team builds & iterates through continuous discovery or similar human-centered design processes.

**Purpose**  
I cultivate product opportunities by aligning user needs to business goals, engaging stakeholders to focus impact, and leading agile teams from ideation through iteration with a relentless focus on the user. 

**What I love doing** 

* Strategy *and* Execution \- Delivery to business outcome  
  - *“Claudia is an awesome product manager who combines strategic breadth with tactical depth. I worked with Claudia while she was responsible for managing Snapfish's expansion into more than 20 international countries, starting with a very small staff initially and growing it to a much larger team. Claudia drove XXXX's expansion with impressive speed and met very aggressive targets.”*  
  - *“Claudia is a product leader who seamlessly blends a deep business background with a clear commitment to a social enterprise's impact.”*  
  - *“She is both a strategic thinker and someone who is willing to get her hands dirty, and do the work needed to move us towards meeting our goals.“*  
  - *She does an excellent job of understanding both the higher level business needs and, when necessary, the project details. She is always concerned about quality for both our customers as well as members of her teams.”*  
* Learning new industries & product methodologies  
  - *“Her mastery of product management runs deep, and while she is never shy to help coach and guide others, she is also a lifelong learner who constantly seeks out best practices to sharpen her game.”*  
* Product Discovery  
  - *“Claudia was a key member of my product team at XXXXXX where she led the retention strategy for the digital experience, and delivered strong business outcomes grounded in deep customer research.”*  
* Ideation   
  - “She is consistently putting the user at the forefront \- driving all of us to think about how different users approach the product, and what each segment is trying to "do" (vs. what we want to teach them).”  
* Visioning  
  - *“In her work with Earn & Learn, she led important conversations using the business model canvas that ultimately helped the organization understand who had the capacity to pay (and who they wanted to serve, but couldn't pay) and focus its product and revenue structure accordingly.”*  
* Collaborating with stakeholders, especially Engineering, UX Design (Agile triad)  
  - *“Claudia is a powerhouse who leads with compassion, authenticity and genuine curiosity.”*   
  - *“She always had an efficient strategy lined up to make our work go smoothly and was excellent in communicating her ideas to the rest of the team. I learned from her even when she wasn’t training me.”*   
  - *“Claudia collaborates well both in person and remotely, and she has a great balance of people skills and product skills.”*  
* Program managing a product/feature launch   
* Secondary research to ground in market/industry/segment/trends/etc.  
* Interviewing users & stakeholders   
* Synthesizing user feedback and looking for themes  
* Co-creating with users/customers to solve problems (ideally using HCD approaches)  
* Thinking through all the use cases, scenarios & downstream impacts & risks  
* People leadership \- especially mentoring junior PMs and/or designers  
  - *“She has single-handedly built our successful International Vertical and created a work environment that reflects her strong management skills and intellect, as well as her heart… She is an advocate for her entire team, yet also cares deeply about each person's professional development (not excluding her own). She genuinely seeks to know who we are as individuals and she cares about what we strive for, and how we can contribute and helps us seize opportunities to grow.”*  
  - *“Claudia brings a rare combination of focus, energy and tireless work ethic. She collaborated with me on recruiting top talent for her team from start to finish. Not only was she effective at communicating a sense of urgency with her team and the candidates, she also articulated expectations and managed the process seamlessly to ensure the acquisition of talent in a timely manner and with a keen eye to every detail. Claudia is a true leader and I highly recommend her.”*  
* Investing in relationships/network and connecting people  
  - *“Finally she is an insatiable learner and connector \- which means that anyone lucky enough to work with Claudia benefits from her advocacy and drive to source resources and answers from colleagues near and far (as an example, while working on product she connected our client with financing and networking opportunities, among others).”*  
* Improving processes–continuous improvement  
  - *“She is not afraid to speak up and honestly share what's on her mind, or push back on the status quo when things don’t make sense.”*  
* Working for a global company (i.e., Internationalization & localization) 

**What I hate doing**

* Redundant and tedious tasks  
* Spreadsheets & pivot tables  
* Financial modeling, too much time coming up with detailed ROI  
* Fundraising  
* Sales / cold calling / pitching, negotiating–I treasure the relationship over the transaction  
* Don’t mind project management, but don’t want it to be \> 30% of my time  
* Full-time management  
  - Managing up to 3 people is ideal (largest \# of people managed: 10 people)  
* Drafting/giving performance reviews  
* Time tracking, expense reporting, etc.  
* Creating project plans in tool like MS Project  
* Writing an exhaustive test plan/UAT criteria  
* Documentation for documentation-sake \- same content in multiple places/tools

**Must-haves** 

* Mission alignment–Looking at: mental health tech, edtech, eldercare, aimed at students/teachers/parent engagement  
* Focused on a clear problem to solve for a particular set of users/customers/patients  
* Need variety in the day-to-day work (don’t want too large a company where role is too narrow/specialized)  
* Ongoing user research (ideally continuous discovery)  
* Strong UX partner/team  
* Product-led organization (Product is on SLT or very close)  
* Manager that cares about me/team & has our back (mutual respect, compassionate, trustworthy, coach, walks the talk)  
* Vision+company strategy I/team can align & plan towards  
* Prefer to be in an environment where strategy/roadmap planning is collaborative  
* Balance of meeting and quiet work time  
* Culture is friendly, collaborative, creative, folks support each other  
* Company is diverse (or actively working towards it)   
* Min 3 weeks vacation  
* Flex hours (I need to get my kids places after school some days)  
* Ideally budget for professional growth opportunities 

**Must-nots**

* Not looking at: social media, fintech, e-commerce, infrastructure (not strong mission alignment for me)  
* Technical PM or Growth PM  
* Extremely early stage startup with inexperienced management team  
* 5 days in office – 2-3 days is perfect  
* Open concept offices (sensory overload)  
* Requires \> 10% travel (Partner is Head of Sales and travels a lot)  
* ‘Too big’ a company (e.g., MANG \- Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon, etc.)  
* Boss as: Micromanager, Idea stealer, Fire drills  
* Don’t want authoritarian or gated leadership culture (prefer flatter hierarchy)  
* Cut-throat culture  
* Lack of transparency & information sharing  
* Ideally not the only product manager unless vision and strategy are clear and leadership is experienced  
* Ask PM to perform 3 different roles: PM \+ UX design \+ project management \+ ScrumMaster, etc.  
* Commute \> :30 each way  
* Manage \> 3-4 people  
* Use waterfall or outdated product/software methodology  
* Inefficient processes and no interest in continuous improvement

**StrengthsFinder Top 5**								

1\. **Futuristic** \- *Bringing your ideas to life* is an exciting proposition for you. You sense you have the power to transform whatever you think is possible into tangible outcomes. *Instinctively, you consistently strive to improve yourself personally and professionally.*  	

2\. **Individualization** \- Intrigued with the unique qualities of each person. They have a gift for *figuring out how people who are different can work together* productively. 	

3\. **Input** \- *Have a craving to know more*. Often they like to collect and archive all kinds of information.  

4\. **Achiever** \- Have a great deal of stamina and work hard. They take great satisfaction from being busy and productive. 

5\. **Learner** \- Have a great desire to learn and want to continuously improve. In particular, the process of learning, rather than the outcome, excites them. 

**Long Term goals**

* Head of Product for smaller social enterprise or nonprofit  
* Take higher impact (likely lower salary) part-time roles or volunteer  
* Join social enterprise or nonprofit boards  
* Mentor diverse women in tech or business

Reflecting back, he said that the combination of forming a JSC along with this exercise and listening tour made the biggest difference, including, importantly, helping him turn down opportunities that were not a great fit.*  Other than creating the JSC itself, the Mnookin Two-Pager was the most crucial step in the process and gave me the most peace of mind in choosing the next step in my career. **Must haves**

* Trust: Manager I trust and can learn from  
* Vision: Purpose and passion \- solving problems for the greater good \- mission over money  
* Company is in growth mode \- hiring not firing  
* Decisive CEO: Do you know the one quality that research has found all billionaires have in common? Decisive leaders are those who seek out the appropriate information that is necessary to make a good decision and they demonstrate an understanding of the knowledge held by their colleagues, direct reports and leaders. In the workplace, decisiveness is key for effectively executing plans and achieving set goals.  
* Focus: Ruthless prioritization of the best / biggest bets that align to customer need and north star metrc success. Not a feature factory. Solutions are not overly complicated and in the weeds \- Simple can be harder than complex: You have to work hard to get your thinking clean to make it simple. But it’s worth it in the end because once you get there, you can move mountains.  
* Leadership   
  * Conviction to the plan   
  * Servant leadership: Do those served grow as persons? Do they, while being served, become healthier, wiser, freer, more autonomous, more likely themselves to become servants? [https://www.behindthemixer.com/servant-leadership/](https://www.behindthemixer.com/servant-leadership/)   
  * Team Development: Promotes building empowered teams. Spends more time growing the team's skills than on the bottomline. Practice, teach and mentor.   
  * Performance judged on outcomes and having a track record of success results in greater autonomy to deliver   
  * Career paths/growth for all  
* Culture  
  * Authentic self  
  * From Daniel Abrahams \- [https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:6809031359458242561/](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:activity:6809031359458242561/)   
    * Work life balance \- Your boss excitedly tells your team she's taking her son to football practice early on Wednesday afternoons. Your kids are welcome to drop-in at any time.  
    * Entrepreneurial not corporate  
    * Fun: You hear laughter, often.  
    * Empathetic \+ compassionate  
    * Diversity \- Your colleagues come from different backgrounds and nationalities.  
    * Talent \- You're rarely the smartest person in a meeting.  
    * Transparency, honesty and candor \- Gossip is shut down quickly.  
    * Listen more than you talk. Nobody learned anything by hearing themselves speak.  
    * Remote \- You're trusted to work from home.  
    * Continuing education outside of work \- Invest in learning  
* How we work  
  * Experimentation \- Innovation and failures are welcomed, not feared.  
  * Product and design thinking  
  * Data driven decision making  
  * Strong triads  
  * Intense Customer Focus: Love client interaction and solving problems but not selling  
  * Disrupt \- Strive to work on something uncomfortably exciting.

**Must nots**

* Corporate compliance  
* Top down feature factory  
* Micromanagement  
* High profile public facing   
* Unnecessary travel  
* Needless documentation \- Endless powerpoints and status updates, business reviews  
* Overly complicated and in the weeds \- Simple can be harder than complex: You have to work hard to get your thinking clean to make it simple. But it’s worth it in the end because once you get there, you can move mountains.  
* Cannot be on campus 9-5 everyday

**What I’m good at that I also love**  
It’s all about the team. I love coaching. I believe a coach’s role is to get the most out of his/her players and to clearly define each of his team members' roles/expectations to accomplish the north star metric. When I look back at my career it has very little to do with the products or features that I have shipped or how much money they have made. It has always been about the feeling of being part of a greater good. The whole being greater than the sum of its parts kind of a thing. Assembling a group of diverse people from various upbringings and educational backgrounds. Working together to solve really challenging problems for humanity. Creating a dynamic environment, with positive energy and excitement to come to stand up everyday because we know what we are working on is meaningful for our customer, the sustainability of the business and the greater good of the team. 

I achieve this by:

* Inspiring and empowering teams with North Star vision/metric.   
* Building trust with servant leadership.   
* Being supportive, I pride myself on allowing my colleagues to have the independence needed to cultivate ideas and try new techniques. I am honest and trusting, which helps me be a mentor for junior staff.  
* Strategic planning: Breaking down vision/missions into actionable strategy using lean canvas frameworks.   
* Team Topology: Constructing teams based on psychological and behavioral need states of each of our team members. I use the Pioneer, Settler, Town Planner methodology which helps identify what different team members prefer to do within the org.   
* Growth Hacking & Experimentation  
  * “Success is sometimes the outcome of a whole string of failures.” Van Gogh  
  * “Teach me something new”   
  * Investing in tech that allows us to get the answers we need  
* KISS: I have a very pragmatic approach to problem solving and prefer simple solutions over needless complexity.   
* Being a bit of a rebel. I am not afraid to upset the status quo if I see an opportunity for improving the business or leadership is moving in a direction i do not agree with

* Motivation by praise and encouragement

* Well-defined goals with strategies to achieve them (buy-in, accountability, milestones)

* XXXX  area or ability to have some face-to-face work/connection

* Travel 2-3 days/week, 2-3 weeks/month

* OTE Comp: $400+

**Must Not**

* Be a company in who’s best days are behind it

* Have a overly political, poorly defined, or non-collaborative culture

* Be in a shrinking market

* Dwell in the past (“we tried it before and it didn’t work, so…”)

* No appetite for investment or for change

* Values misalignment

* Require a relocation

* Be fully remote

* Expect routine weekend travel

## CEO {#ceo}

### CEO of Consumer Internet {#ceo-of-consumer-internet}

| *Below is a simple Mnookin Two-Pager developed by an experienced consumer Internet CEO looking for his next role (he had recently moved from CEO to Board Chair of his current company). Note that in his goals he included a very important personal goal of being present for his teenage children. He’s also quite committed to a multiple stakeholder view of a company’s responsibilities (i.e., not just to shareholders, but to employees, customers, and community) and notes that he won’t accept a Board of Directors (BOD) role if a company only focuses on shareholders.* |
| :---- |

**My goals**

* Lock down path to generate minimum cash comp to avoid burning equity savings (for next 3-5 years or until \[Current Company\] equity becomes more liquid). Could be CEO or multiple Board roles  
* Be present for children in these next 2-4 formative teenage years  
* Create a platform for broader messaging around 4-stakeholder management (executive social responsibility)

**Love doing**

* Working on more sophisticated networked business models (networks vs. traditional commerce)  
* Building a strong culture and environment where people look back and say ‘best team and culture ever’ (success at last 3 jobs)  
* Driving mindset change around the role of the executive vis-a-vis societal impact (4th  
  stakeholder)

**Hate Doing**

* Politics and bureaucracy of a large company  
* Unnecessary drama  
* Being micromanaged

**Must Haves**

* CEO of a large scale or imminently large-scale (user footprint) B2B/SMB internet business (not selling to Enterprises)  
* Large market with strategy to win or ability to redirect strategy to win  
* Compensation:

  * If CEO path: minimum $500K total potential cash flow  
  * If Board-only path: Minimum supplemental cash flow of $300K

**Must Nots:**

* Not moving from Bay Area and can’t be gone more than 2 nights a week on a typical commute cycle  
* BOD or bosses with low trust / low integrity / only shareholder focus (need to be able to set culture aligned to 4th-stakeholder approach)  
* Distressed/turnaround unless there is *significant* cash/equity offset that hedges downside risks (e.g. stock ownership vs. options)
